description: Iconic parian china made on the banks of the Erne in Northern Ireland since 1857, using methods passed down for generations.
evidence_note: All making at the Belleek works, Co. Fermanagh; parian body mineral sourcing not publicly evidenced — Silver pending confirmation.

name: Clive Bowen (Shebbear Pottery)

name: Jim Malone
description: Stoneware in the Leach-Hamada line, made in the Eden Valley with clays, granites and wood ash gathered from the Cumbrian landscape.

name: Matthew Blakely
address: Fen-edge village near Cambridge, Cambridgeshire, CB25 9EP
description: Pots made entirely from rocks and clays collected at named British locations — each piece is literally made of its landscape.
evidence_note: Bodies and glazes made from UK geological samples he collects and processes himself; clays often used as dug; wood-fired. CPA member.

name: Fitch & McAndrew
address: Workshop near Corsock, Dumfries & Galloway, DG7 3ED
description: Doug Fitch and Hannah McAndrew's wood-fired slipware — honey-glazed earthenware in the great British country pottery tradition.
evidence_note: All made at their Galloway workshop; red earthenware body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA members.

name: Micki Schloessingk (Bridge Pottery)
address: Bridge Pottery, Cheriton, Gower, Swansea SA3 1BY
description: Wood-fired, salt-glazed pots made on the Gower peninsula since 1987; work held by the V&A. Gallery open to visitors.
evidence_note: Made and wood-fired at Cheriton, but stoneware clay imported from St Amand, France — a clear imported-body Silver. CPA member.

name: David & Margaret Frith (Brookhouse Pottery)
address: Brookhouse Pottery, Brookhouse Lane, Denbigh LL16 4RE
description: Half a century of reduction-fired stoneware and porcelain from a converted mill in Denbigh; showroom on site.
evidence_note: All made at the Denbigh workshop; clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA fellows.

name: Lisa Hammond (Maze Hill Pottery)
address: Maze Hill Pottery, The Old Ticket Office, Woodlands Park Road, Greenwich SE10, SE10 9XE
description: Soda-glazed functional pots from the old ticket office at Maze Hill station, by Lisa Hammond MBE, co-founder of Clay College Stoke.
evidence_note: Thrown and soda-fired in Greenwich; clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA fellow.

name: Sasha Wardell
description: Layered, slip-cast bone china of exceptional delicacy, made and taught from a Wiltshire studio.
evidence_note: Slip-cast and finished at her Wiltshire studio; bone-china body source not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA member.

name: Jane Hamlyn (Millfield Pottery)
description: Salt-glazed functional pottery of quiet authority, made at Millfield Pottery since 1975.
evidence_note: Made and salt-fired at Everton; clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA fellow.

name: Walter Keeler
description: Salt-glazed and Whieldon-ware pots with a wit all their own, from one of Britain's most influential living potters.
evidence_note: Made at his Monmouthshire workshop; clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA fellow.

name: Sandy Brown
description: Exuberant, colourful tableware and large-scale ceramic art from a studio-gallery on the Appledore quayside.
evidence_note: Made at her Appledore studio; clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA fellow.

name: John Pollex
description: Vividly coloured contemporary slipware, painted with slips like an abstract canvas, made in Plymouth since the 1970s.
evidence_note: Thrown and decorated at his Plymouth studio; clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA fellow.

name: Penny Simpson
description: Handthrown tableware with lively slip decoration, made on the edge of Dartmoor; workshop and showroom open to visitors.
evidence_note: Made at her Moretonhampstead workshop; clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA member.

name: Chris Keenan
description: Precise, serene tableware and bowls in tenmoku and celadon, thrown in London by Edmund de Waal's first apprentice.
evidence_note: Thrown and fired in London, famously in Limoges porcelain — a clear imported-body Silver. CPA fellow.

name: Sue Paraskeva
address: Studio on the Isle of Wight
description: Altered porcelain vessels and restaurant tableware, thrown and gas-fired in an Isle of Wight studio.
evidence_note: Made on the Isle of Wight; porcelain body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA member.

name: Akiko Hirai
address: The Chocolate Factory, Stoke Newington, London N16
description: Moon jars and quietly poetic functional ware from a Stoke Newington studio; among Britain's most collected potters.
evidence_note: Made at her London studio; clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA member.

name: James & Tilla Waters
description: Immaculate thrown tableware and one-off pieces from a hillside workshop in rural Carmarthenshire.
evidence_note: Made at their Carmarthenshire workshop; clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA members.

name: Jack Doherty
description: Soda-fired porcelain vessels in luminous colour, by the former lead potter of the Leach Pottery.
evidence_note: Made and soda-fired in Cornwall; porcelain body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA fellow.

name: Adam Buick
address: Studio near St Davids, Pembrokeshire, SA62 6QY
description: Moon jars mapping the Pembrokeshire landscape, often incorporating locally gathered stone and clay inclusions.
evidence_note: Made in Pembrokeshire, with local materials used in some work; base body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA member.

name: Nicola Werner
address: Studio at Hemyock, Blackdown Hills, Devon, TA4 3JT
description: Hand-painted majolica tableware in the English country tradition, from a Blackdown Hills smallholding.
evidence_note: Made and painted at her Devon workshop; earthenware body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA member.

name: Katharina Klug
description: Naked-raku and thrown porcelain vessels with graphite-line decoration, made in Cambridge.
evidence_note: Made at her Cambridge studio; porcelain body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation. CPA member.

name: Churchill China
address: Marlborough Pottery, High Street, Tunstall, Stoke-on-Trent ST6 5NZ
description: Making tableware in Stoke since 1795 — the super-vitrified ware trusted by restaurants everywhere, now sold for home tables too.
evidence_note: Manufactured in Stoke-on-Trent (company pages); clay-body sourcing not publicly evidenced — Silver pending confirmation.

name: Cornishware (T.G. Green)
address: T.G. Green pottery, Somerset; bisque ware made in Stoke-on-Trent
description: The iconic blue-and-white striped kitchenware, back to 100% UK production — bisque made in Stoke, decorated and glazed in the West Country.
evidence_note: Company states 100% UK production using traditional Cornish clay; owner bought the Royal Stafford factory (2025) to secure UK bisque supply.

name: Littlethorpe Potteries
description: Working country pottery since 1831 and the only pottery in Britain still continuously digging its clay on site — thrown terracotta from its own seam.
evidence_note: The only UK pottery continuously digging its raw clay on-site (pit 800m from the pottery); all making on site.

name: Errington Reay
description: Britain's last commercial salt-glazed pottery, hand-throwing garden pots at Bardon Mill since 1878.
evidence_note: All thrown and salt-fired at Bardon Mill; historically local clay mines, current body source not publicly evidenced — Silver pending confirmation.

name: ANTA
description: Hand-painted tartan and thistle spongeware stoneware, made almost entirely by hand at Fearn in the Highlands for 40 years.
evidence_note: Stoneware made and hand-painted at the Fearn pottery (company pages); clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation.

name: Crail Pottery
description: Three generations of the Grieve family throwing stoneware, terracotta and raku in a courtyard pottery in the East Neuk of Fife.
evidence_note: Every piece thrown, decorated, glazed and fired at the Crail workshops; clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation.

name: Ballydougan Pottery
description: Hand-thrown Irish stoneware made at a 1785 thatched homestead near Craigavon since 1984.
evidence_note: Handmade at the Ballydougan workshops, Co. Armagh; clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation.

name: Sheila Fleet
address: Sheila Fleet Kirk Gallery, Tankerness, Orkney KW17 2QT
description: Enamelled silver, gold and platinum jewellery designed, made and finished at a workshop by the sea in Orkney, by Sheila Fleet OBE.
evidence_note: Company states all jewellery is designed, made and finished at the Tankerness workshop; hand-enamelling visible to visitors.

name: Ola Gorie
description: The jeweller who started Orkney's modern jewellery tradition in 1960 — Norse and Pictish-inspired pieces made in Kirkwall.
evidence_note: Making in Orkney since 1960; bench evidence lighter than Fleet's — Gold at medium confidence, worth confirming workshop details.

name: Deakin & Francis
description: England's oldest family jewellers — cufflinks and signets hand-crafted in the same Jewellery Quarter factory since 1786.
evidence_note: Company states all products are hand-crafted at its Birmingham Jewellery Quarter factory.

name: Hamilton & Inches
description: Edinburgh silversmiths and jewellers since 1866, with working gold and silver workshops above the George Street showroom.
evidence_note: Maintains on-site silversmithing and goldsmithing workshops in Edinburgh; extent of in-house vs bought-in ranges worth confirming.

name: Alex Monroe
description: Nature-inspired jewellery — the famous bumblebee — designed and handmade above the Snowsfields boutique in Southwark since 1986.
evidence_note: Company states every piece is designed and handmade at the London studio, with a stated commitment to making in England.

name: C W Sellors
description: Britain's champion of native gemstones — Derbyshire Blue John and Whitby jet cut and set at its own Derbyshire workshops; owns Whitby's W Hamond.
evidence_note: Manufactures at its Ashbourne workshops since 1979; works UK-mined stones (Blue John, Whitby jet) — UK material plus UK making.

name: Rhiannon
address: The Welsh Gold Centre, The Square, Tregaron SY25 6JL
description: Celtic jewellery hand-crafted in the Welsh-speaking heart of Ceredigion since 1971, using genuinely Welsh gold of Gwynfynydd provenance.
evidence_note: Hand-crafted in Wales at Tregaron since 1971; Welsh gold blend of authenticated Gwynfynydd (UK-mined) provenance.

name: Hebridean Jewellery
address: Iochdar, Isle of South Uist HS8 5QX
description: Celtic jewellery made by the silver sands of South Uist in the Outer Hebrides since 1974 — one of Britain's most remote workshops.
evidence_note: Manufactured at the Iochdar workshop, South Uist, since 1974 (company and tourism-board pages).

name: Roger W. Smith
address: Studio on the Isle of Man (British Isles)
description: Britain's greatest living watchmaker, making watches almost entirely in-house on the Isle of Man in the Daniels tradition — a handful a year.
evidence_note: Movements, dials and cases substantially made in-house on the Isle of Man (Crown dependency — included by the map's British Isles policy).

name: Charles Frodsham & Co
address: 32 Bury Street, St James's, London SW1Y 6AU
description: The oldest continuously trading chronometer maker in the world — its Double Impulse wristwatch is the first fully in-house English wristwatch in generations.
evidence_note: Movement designed and made in-house in England over a 16-year development; London shop, Sussex workshops.

name: Garrick Watchmakers
description: High-end English watchmaking in Norfolk — enamel dials, hands and movement parts made in-house, cases manufactured locally.
evidence_note: Dials, hands and many movement parts made at the Norfolk workshop; UT-G01 movement hand-built in Norfolk (developed with Swiss partner UhrTeil); some models use Swiss base movements — Gold at medium confidence.

name: anOrdain
description: Glasgow studio famous for grand feu enamel dials made entirely in-house — rare craft, honest pricing.
evidence_note: Enamel dials made and watches assembled in Glasgow; Swiss movements — genuine UK making around an imported movement.

name: Bremont
address: The Wing, Reading Road, Henley-on-Thames RG9 1LR
description: Aviation-inspired chronometers from The Wing at Henley — the first purpose-built British watchmaking facility in generations.
evidence_note: Case and movement components assembled and finished at Henley; movements not fully UK-made — Silver under the watch rule.

name: Fears
description: Bristol's revived family watch company (est. 1846), hand-assembling its watches in the city again.
evidence_note: Assembly at its Bristol premises with Swiss movements — Silver; workshop details worth confirming directly.

name: Mourne Textiles
description: Three generations hand-weaving throws, scarves and fabric at the foot of the Mournes since 1949 — mid-century designs still made on the original looms.
evidence_note: Fabric handwoven at the Killowen workshop — the weaving (milling) is the UK transformation; natural fibres spun locally per company.

name: Thomas Ferguson Irish Linen
description: The last of the old Irish linen jacquard weavers, weaving damask in Banbridge since 1854.
evidence_note: Linen woven at the Banbridge mill from 100% flax yarns — fabric milled in UK (raw flax fibre imported, per rulebook fine).

name: Ballylagan Organic Farm
description: Northern Ireland's first organic farm shop — the sole outlet for the 120-acre farm's own beef, pork, bacon, eggs, fruit and veg.
evidence_note: Shop is the sole outlet for all home-grown produce (company pages); some grocery lines stocked alongside.

name: Eden Pottery
description: Sponge-printed pottery made at a countryside studio on the Ards Peninsula, with shop and café on site.
evidence_note: Ware made and decorated at the Millisle studio; clay-body origin not stated — Silver pending confirmation.

name: The Steensons
address: Toberwine Street, Glenarm BT44 0AP (also Bedford Street, Belfast)
description: Northern Ireland's leading contemporary jewellery makers, hand-crafting in the seaside village of Glenarm for over forty years — including the Game of Thrones jewellery.
evidence_note: Visitors can watch craftspeople cut, shape and work the metals at the Glenarm workshop; family firm, second generation.

name: Faller
description: Family jewellers since 1883, designing and making their own collections in the workshop above the Strand Road shop.
evidence_note: Designs and makes own jewellery in the on-site Derry workshop (company history); an early adopter of in-house laser welding with the Steensons.

name: Nomadic Watches
address: Boutique & workshop by City Hall, Belfast, BT1 5HD
description: Belfast's watch brand, named for the Titanic's tender ship — tool watches hand-assembled at the workshop beside City Hall.
evidence_note: Watches hand-assembled in Belfast around Swiss Sellita movements — genuine UK assembly, imported movement: Silver under the watch rule.

name: Yarmouth Oilskins
description: Workwear made in the same Great Yarmouth factory since 1898 — smocks, jackets and trousers cut from British-milled cotton.
evidence_note: Made in its own Great Yarmouth factory; cotton from UK mills incl. Carrington Textiles (Lancashire), dyed by Pincroft, Adlington.

name: Farfield Clothing
address: The Old British School, Sedbergh, Cumbria, LA10 5AS
description: Fleeces, gilets and jackets made in a Victorian schoolhouse in Sedbergh since 1980.
evidence_note: Manufactured in Sedbergh from fabric made exclusively for them by one of the last remaining Yorkshire mills.

name: Troy London
description: Wax jackets and country staples for town and field, made in the UK.
evidence_note: Wax jackets made entirely in the UK from 100% cotton milled in England with a dry wax finish.

name: McNair Shirts
description: Merino mountain shirts hand-made in a Pennine mill — arguably the shortest supply chain in British clothing.
evidence_note: Cloth dyed, spun, woven, milled and finished within 10 miles of the Slaithwaite atelier where the shirts are made.

name: Fieldware Co
description: Waxed cotton aprons and workwear for makers and growers, handcrafted in Somerset.
evidence_note: Handcrafted in Somerset from waxed cotton milled by Halley Stevensons of Dundee, weaving and waxing since 1864.

name: Hegarty
description: Sustainable tailored outerwear made in London in English cloth.
evidence_note: All garments made in London using English fabrics — e.g. the overcoat in 100% English wool tweed.

name: Lochcarron of Scotland
description: The world's leading tartan weaver — over 500 tartans woven at its own Borders mill.
evidence_note: Yarn spun in Yorkshire, then dyed, warped, woven and finished at Lochcarron's own Selkirk mill.

name: Berk
description: Burlington Arcade cashmere house whose knitwear is frame-knitted in the Scottish Borders.
evidence_note: Cashmere spun in Scotland and knitted stitch-by-stitch on frames in the Borders by former Ballantyne hands; 48 hand processes.

name: Colhay's
description: Mid-century-weight lambswool and cashmere knitwear, hand-linked in Hawick.
evidence_note: Yarn spun by Todd & Duncan at Loch Leven, knitted and hand-linked by a Hawick knitter (a few pieces made in Japan).

name: Malloch's
description: Luxury knitwear made in Hawick from yarn spun by Britain's best-known spinners.
evidence_note: Knitted in Hawick from yarn spun by Todd & Duncan (Kinross), Z. Hinchliffe (Denby Dale) and J.C. Rennie (Aberdeenshire).

name: Glenbrae
address: Spa Mill, Slaithwaite, West Yorkshire, HD7 5BB
description: Golf and classic knitwear made in England by a mill that spins its own yarn.
evidence_note: Designed and manufactured in England by Spectrum Yarns at Spa Mill, which spins its own Spirol lambswool/merino yarn on site.

name: Michael Ross
description: Hand-framed Fair Isle knitwear with up to eleven colours in a row — impossible on automatic machines.
evidence_note: Hand-frame knitted in Thatcham using wool from Yorkshire, Scotland and Ireland.

name: Oubas
description: Small-batch knitwear made in a Cumbrian studio from local fleece.
evidence_note: Knitted in their own Ulverston studio; certified British Wool manufacturing partner using local fleece and UK woollen mills.

name: Mars Knitwear
description: Leicester knitwear manufacturer making its own range in 100% British wool.
evidence_note: Knitted and finished in-house at Wigston since 1994 using 100% British wool yarn from local British spinners.

name: Glencroft
description: Yorkshire Dales countrywear, with own-brand jumpers in wool from farms within five miles.
evidence_note: Own-brand knitwear made in Britain from Clapdale yarn scoured, carded and spun in Yorkshire from local farms. Shop also stocks imported goods.

name: Izzy Lane
description: Knitwear from a flock of 700 rescued Wensleydale and Shetland sheep — no animal is slaughtered.
evidence_note: Wool from her own rescued flock, spun by a Calderdale worsted spinner, made up in West Yorkshire and the Scottish Borders.

name: Navygrey
description: One perfect jumper, made properly — Scottish-spun lambswool knitted in Britain.
evidence_note: Signature jumpers use 100% Scottish-spun lambswool, knitted and hand-finished in Britain; newer linen/cotton lines less clearly UK-made.

name: Eas Fors
description: Knitwear made start to finish on the Isle of Mull in superfine Scottish lambswool.
evidence_note: Machine knitted and hand finished entirely on Mull using lambswool spun on the banks of Loch Leven.

name: Carnwear
description: Cornish knitwear fully-fashioned on hand-powered machines.
evidence_note: Made in their own Penzance studio (finer gauges knitted 8 miles away in St Ives); many products British Wool certified.

name: Quinton + Chadwick
description: Knitted accessories in lambswool, merino and recycled cashmere, made at British heritage mills.
evidence_note: Knitted at heritage mills in Scotland, Nottingham and Devon; company states it uses British mills for yarn supplies.

name: The Croft House
description: Scotland's first B Corp certified wool knitwear brand.
evidence_note: Made in Scotland using only natural wool and cashmere spun in British mills.

name: Goral
description: Third-generation Sheffield shoemakers, resoleable shoes handmade in their own workshop.
evidence_note: Every pair handmade in the family's Sheffield workshop with leather from Charles F. Stead's tannery in Leeds.

name: Billy Tannery
description: Runs Britain's only goatskin micro-tannery, turning a waste by-product into leather goods.
evidence_note: Tans British goat and deer skins itself at its own micro-tannery, then has bags handmade in Britain; Heritage Crafts sustainability award 2025.

name: Cherchbi
description: Bags in Herdwyck tweed woven from Cumbrian fell-sheep fleece.
evidence_note: Made by Mowbray Leather Goods, Melton Mowbray, from its own Herdwyck No.10 tweed (Cumbrian Herdwick wool woven in Wales) and English veg-tanned saddle leather.

name: McRostie of Glasgow
description: Glasgow leather workshop trading since 1887, everything made to order in Scotland.
evidence_note: Every bag and belt made to order in Scotland from traditionally pit-tanned British bridle leather.

description: Relaunched cotton label carrying the name of Tower Mill, the last cotton spinner in England.
evidence_note: UK spinning ceased when the parent company was liquidated in 2024; relaunched 2026 as clothing designed, cut, sewn and finished in the UK from bought-in fabric.

name: G.H. Hurt & Son
description: Knitted lace shawls made in Nottingham since 1912 — the christening shawl of choice for royal babies.
evidence_note: Knitted and hand-finished in their Nottingham factory, but merino yarn comes from spinners in both Britain and Italy — UK yarn not assured.

name: House of Cheviot
description: Shooting and country socks knitted, linked and hand-finished in Hawick.
evidence_note: Made in Hawick, but the Australian merino is spun in Italy and the cashmere combed in Mongolia.

name: &Daughter
description: Knitwear rooted in the family's Irish and Scottish knitting heritage.
evidence_note: Yarn spun by Todd & Duncan in Scotland, but knitting is split across makers in the Scottish Borders and Donegal, Ireland — UK share unproven.

name: Woolkind
description: Made-to-order merino knitwear from an Edinburgh studio — no stock, no waste.
evidence_note: Knitted to order in their Marchmont studio, but the superfine merino is washed, dyed and spun in Biella, Italy.

name: London Tradition
address: Wallis Road, Hackney Wick, London E9, E9 5LN
description: One of London's last coat factories, turning out up to a thousand duffle, pea and trench coats a week.
evidence_note: Cut, sewn and finished by hand at the Wallis Road factory, but the signature double-faced duffle cloth is Italian.

name: Grenfell
description: The cloth that clothed Everest and the poles, still made up into coats in an east London factory.
evidence_note: All garments made in Grenfell's own east London factory; no current evidence that Grenfell Cloth is still woven in Britain since Lodge Mill, Burnley.

name: Gloverall
description: The company that turned the naval duffle coat into a British classic in 1951.
evidence_note: Only the Heritage Collection is stated as made in England, and the Original Monty uses Italian wool; the wider range is not UK-made.

name: Yarmo
description: Traditional British workwear — warehouse coats, smocks and dungarees — made in Norfolk since 1898.
evidence_note: Manufactured in Great Yarmouth since 1898, but no published evidence of UK-milled cloth for the current range.

name: Buffalo Systems
description: The Pertex-and-pile system that keeps British mountaineers alive, sewn in Sheffield.
evidence_note: Everything still sewn at the Sheffield factory, but Pertex has been made in Japan since Perseverance Mills, Padiham closed in 2005.

name: Aero Leather Clothing
description: Reproduction flight and motorcycle jackets, hand-made in a Borders mill.
evidence_note: Jackets hand-made at Greenbank Mill, Galashiels, but hides are American front-quarter and Italian vegetable-tanned horsehide.

name: Fox Umbrellas
description: The umbrella maker to diplomats and film sets, hand-made to order in Croydon.
evidence_note: Each umbrella hand-made to order at the Croydon factory, but the canopy cloth has no evidenced UK weaving origin.

name: Budd Shirts
address: Workroom in Andover; shop in Piccadilly Arcade, London
description: Piccadilly Arcade shirtmaker since 1910, with its own English workroom.
evidence_note: Ready-to-wear and made-to-measure shirts cut and sewn at Budd's Andover workroom; shirtings from Swiss and Italian mills.

name: Fortis
description: Outdoor and workwear handmade to order in a converted lambing barn on the family farm.
evidence_note: Handmade to order in Devon; the company states only that it 'aims' to buy all fabric in the UK.

name: Gushlow & Cole
description: Shearling and leather outerwear, designed and made within thirty miles of the Kent workshop.
evidence_note: All design, sampling and production in their Kent workshop or within 30 miles, but shearling is tanned by Iberian tanneries.

name: British Sheepskin
description: Sheepskin coats hand-cut and made to order in a Somerset workshop.
evidence_note: Every coat hand-cut and made to order in Somerset, but skins are imported merino, Toscana and Mongolian shearling.

name: Lockwood Smocks
description: Technical smocks handmade in North Devon for people who work outdoors.
evidence_note: Handmade in Barnstaple, but the main fabric is PU-coated Cordura nylon with no evidenced UK weaving.

name: Darzi Clothing Company
description: Men's outerwear and accessories, with production brought back from India to England in 2015.
evidence_note: Made in England since 2015, but cloth is sourced from independent mills across the UK and Europe, so UK milling isn't established.

name: Thorndale
description: Country bags and cases handcrafted in the same Staffordshire factory since 1957.
evidence_note: Handcrafted in their own Staffordshire factory; waxed styles use British waxed cotton but the ballistic nylon's origin is unstated.

name: Palava
description: Hand-drawn prints on dresses and coats, cut and sewn in a family-run East London factory.
evidence_note: Made in a family-run Barking factory, but the printed fabrics are woven, dyed and printed in Turkey.

name: Crown Northampton
description: Northampton's sneaker specialists — hand-lasted trainers and boots from their own factory.
evidence_note: Made in their own Northampton factory, but uppers are sourced from tanneries worldwide including Horween (Chicago) alongside C.F. Stead.

name: Sanders & Sanders
description: Family Goodyear-welted shoemakers in Rushden since 1873.
evidence_note: Entire collection Goodyear-welted at the family's Spencer Road factory; no evidence of UK-tanned upper leather.

name: William Lennon & Co
address: The Old Corn Mill, Stoney Middleton, Derbyshire, S32 4TD
description: Boots and clogs made in a Peak District corn mill since 1904.
evidence_note: Made in the Old Corn Mill since 1904, but upper leather now comes from Horween, Chicago (formerly Bridge of Weir); only sole leather is Northampton-tanned.

name: John Lobb (St James's)
description: The independent family bootmaker on St James's Street — bespoke only, entirely by hand.
evidence_note: Wholly hand-made in the London workshop; calf bought in from Continental tanneries, no UK tannery evidenced.

name: Dartmoor Shoemakers (Green Shoes)
description: Made-to-order shoes and boots from a Dartmoor workshop, repairable for life.
evidence_note: Hand-made to order in the Devon workshop, but the firm states it uses Italian leather.

name: Owen Barry
description: Sheepskin and leather bags made in Somerset's shoemaking town since 1948.
evidence_note: Cut and sewn at the Street factory since 1948; materials described only as British or European from unnamed tanneries.

name: Cambridge Satchel Company
description: The kitchen-table startup that became a British classic, made in its own Leicestershire factory.
evidence_note: Bags made in their own Leicestershire factory, but leather comes from a Dutch supplier as well as two UK tanneries.

name: The Leather Satchel Co
description: Family workshop hand-making satchels on Merseyside since 1966.
evidence_note: Hand-made in the family Knowsley workshop, but leathers come from British, Italian and Dutch tanneries plus Horween cordovan.

name: Broadland Slippers
description: Traditional hand-lasted slippers made in Norwich.
evidence_note: Hand-cut and lasted in Norwich using traditional methods; no origin evidence for the velvets and leathers used.

name: Barnwell Footwear
description: Father-and-son moccasin makers in the Northamptonshire shoe country.
evidence_note: Made in their own Kettering workshop, claiming all components sourced in the UK, but no tannery is named.

name: Zatchels
description: Hand-made leather satchels and bags, made to order in Leicester.
evidence_note: Handmade to order in Leicester by Britannia Hide, which cites leather from 'a Scottish tannery' — tannery unnamed, so Gold not evidenced.

name: JuJu Footwear
description: The original British jelly shoe, moulded in Northampton since 1986.
evidence_note: Injection-moulded in JuJu's own Northampton factory; materials described as 'sourced in England' rather than UK-produced.

name: Swaine (Swaine Adeney Brigg)
description: Bridle-leather cases and Brigg umbrellas, by royal appointment since 1750.
evidence_note: Hand-stitched at the Sawston factory and Brigg umbrellas made in Cambridgeshire; 'English bridle leather' claimed but no tannery named.

name: De Winter
description: Goodyear-welted boots made by Northamptonshire hands.
evidence_note: No factory of its own; boots hand-cut and Goodyear-welted by Northamptonshire contract makers, leather unspecified.

name: Percy Stride
description: Goodyear-welted men's shoes made in Northampton at an accessible price.
evidence_note: Made for the brand by a small family-run Northampton factory; leather origin unstated.

name: Arthur Sleep

description: The world's oldest hat shop, blocking and finishing hats in St James's since 1676.

description: Belts made start to finish at their own Rutland factory.

name: Church's
description: Northampton shoemaker since 1873, still Goodyear-welting at the St James factory.

name: Grenson
description: Northamptonshire shoemaker since 1866, with English-made welted collections.

name: Barker Shoes
description: Hand-lasted Goodyear-welted shoes made at the Earls Barton factory since 1880.

description: Yorkshire bootmaker producing military and hiking boots at its Richmond factory.

description: Sheffield maker of steel goods, leather and clothing rooted in Peak District cycling.

name: Freddies of Pinewood

name: Peper Harow
